explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Abram says, "…since I remain childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?" (Genesis 15:2). He's holding the biggest empty spot in his tent up to God. I think that's a hard thing to say out loud, and he says it anyway.

Good guess, friend, because livestock was a big deal for a man like Abram. But he never mentions animals here. What he says is, "…since I remain childless…" (Genesis 15:2). The empty spot isn't in the pasture, it's in the house.

Silver is a fair thing to think of when somebody asks "what can You give me?" But Abram doesn't bring up money at all. He says, "…since I remain childless…" (Genesis 15:2). What he lacks is a child, not a coin.

Yes, friend! Abram says, "…a servant in my household will be my heir." (Genesis 15:3). Without a child, the house goes to someone already living in it. I think Abram says it plainly because he's laying out his problem for God.

A cousin sounds like a sensible pick, I'll give you that. But Abram doesn't name any relative here. He says, "…a servant in my household will be my heir." (Genesis 15:3). Nobody from the family tree shows up in this verse.

A brother makes sense on paper, friend. But Abram never mentions one in this conversation. He says, "…a servant in my household will be my heir." (Genesis 15:3). The person he has in mind is somebody who works in his own house.

Not this time, baker. Abram says Eliezer will be his heir, but God answers, "This one will not be your heir, but one who comes from your own body will be your heir." (Genesis 15:4). God says it right back to him, plain as day. The answer is False, and it's good news.

That's right, friend! God tells Abram, "This one will not be your heir, but one who comes from your own body will be your heir." (Genesis 15:4). Abram names Eliezer, and God says no, not him. God gives a clear answer to Abram's worry.

Yes, baker! "Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able." (Genesis 15:5). God takes him outside and points him at the whole sky. I bet counting stops somewhere around star number twelve for most of us.

That's the one, friend. God says, "So shall your offspring be." (Genesis 15:5). Abram has no child at that moment, and God points to a sky full of stars. I think that's a lot to take in standing in the dark.

Sand does show up later in Abraham's story, but not in this verse. Here, God says, "Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able." (Genesis 15:5). The picture is stars overhead, not sand underfoot.

Flocks make sense for a man who lived with animals, friend. But God never mentions them here. He says, "Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able." (Genesis 15:5). The count is up in the sky.

Tents were everywhere in Abram's world, so I see why you'd pick it. But God sends his eyes upward, not around the camp. He says, "Now look to the heavens and count the stars, if you are able." (Genesis 15:5).
That's it, baker. "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness." (Genesis 15:6). Nothing about his tent had changed yet. He still had no child, and he believed anyway.
Abram does build altars in other places, friend, but not here. This verse says, "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness." (Genesis 15:6). What he does is believe.

I get why you'd think that, since Abram just asked a heavy question. But the text doesn't say he walks off worried. It says, "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness." (Genesis 15:6). He believes, and that's the whole verse.
Right, friend! God says He brought Abram out of Ur "to give you this land to possess." (Genesis 15:7). Ur of the Chaldeans was where the trip started. God tells him where it was headed.
A king would be a big title, I'll give you that. But God doesn't say it here. He says He brought Abram out of Ur "to give you this land to possess." (Genesis 15:7). The promise is about land.
Priest is a fair guess, baker, but it isn't in this verse. God says He brought Abram out of Ur "to give you this land to possess." (Genesis 15:7). The gift God names is the land.

explanations.answer: How he can know he will possess it
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Abram asks, "Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?" (Genesis 15:8). It's an honest question, asked right to God. I think it's the kind of thing a person says out loud when they want to be sure.

explanations.answer: How far its borders will reach
explanations.explanation: Borders come up later, but Abram doesn't ask about them. He asks, "Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?" (Genesis 15:8). His question is about knowing it'll really happen.

explanations.answer: When his family should move there
explanations.explanation: Moving day is a sensible thing to wonder about, friend. But Abram doesn't ask about timing. He asks, "Lord GOD, how can I know that I will possess it?" (Genesis 15:8). He wants to know how he can be sure.

That's right, baker. God asked for "a heifer, a goat, and a ram, each three years old, along with a turtledove and a young pigeon." (Genesis 15:9). Then "Abram brought all these to Him…" (Genesis 15:10). He brings the whole list, no shortcuts.

Not quite, friend. After God lists the heifer, goat, ram, turtledove and young pigeon (Genesis 15:9), the text says, "So Abram brought all these to Him…" (Genesis 15:10). Nothing on the list is missing. The answer is True.
Not this time, baker. The birds of prey do come down, but "…Abram drove them away." (Genesis 15:11). He doesn't let them have a thing. The answer is False.
Yes, friend! "And the birds of prey descended on the carcasses, but Abram drove them away." (Genesis 15:11). He stays and keeps the animals safe. I think that's a long watch, and he does it anyway.

That's right, baker. God says, "But I will judge the nation they serve as slaves…" (Genesis 15:14). He speaks about the very place where Abram's descendants will be enslaved. God doesn't leave that hardship unanswered.
Not this time, friend. God says, "But I will judge the nation they serve as slaves…" (Genesis 15:14). He says it plainly, right after naming the slavery. The answer is True.

explanations.answer: They will depart with many possessions
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, "…afterward they will depart with many possessions." (Genesis 15:14). They don't just get out. They walk out carrying a lot with them.

explanations.answer: They will stay and rule over that nation
explanations.explanation: Ruling is a big turnaround, I get the thought. But God doesn't say it. He says, "…afterward they will depart with many possessions." (Genesis 15:14). The word is depart, not rule.

explanations.answer: They will scatter among the other nations
explanations.explanation: Scattering is a real thing that happens to people in the Bible, friend, but it's not what God says here. He says, "…afterward they will depart with many possessions." (Genesis 15:14). They leave, and they leave with a lot.

That's it, baker. God tells Abram, "You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age." (Genesis 15:15). After hearing about hard years ahead for his descendants, Abram gets this word for himself. I think that's a comfort.

I see why you'd think that, since the words before it are heavy. But God says, "You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age." (Genesis 15:15). For Abram himself, the word is peace.

Exile fits the hard news about his descendants, friend. But God says something different about Abram: "You, however, will go to your fathers in peace and be buried at a ripe old age." (Genesis 15:15). The word is peace.

explanations.answer: Their sin is not yet complete
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. God says, "…for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete." (Genesis 15:16). Iniquity means sin. That's the reason He gives for why the return isn't sooner.

explanations.answer: Their cities are not yet built
explanations.explanation: Cities are a reasonable guess, but God doesn't mention them. He says, "…for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete." (Genesis 15:16). The reason has to do with their sin.

explanations.answer: Their army is not yet weak
explanations.explanation: An army is the kind of thing you'd think of, friend. But God doesn't say that here. He says, "…for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete." (Genesis 15:16). It's about their sin, not their soldiers.

Not quite, baker. The text says the firepot and torch "passed between the halves of the carcasses." (Genesis 15:17). They go through the middle, between the halves Abram laid out. The answer is False.
That's right, friend! "…a smoking firepot and a flaming torch appeared and passed between the halves of the carcasses." (Genesis 15:17). They go down the middle, through the path between the halves.

Yes, baker! "On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram…" (Genesis 15:18). Abram asked how he could know, and this is what happens that day. A covenant is a solemn promise, and this one is God's.

A new name does come for Abram, friend, but later in his story and not in this passage. Here it says, "On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram…" (Genesis 15:18). That's what happens when the firepot and torch pass through.
A feast sounds nice, and I'm not going to argue with that. But this passage doesn't have one. It says, "On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram…" (Genesis 15:18).
